subject: Biology
title: Yeast and Fermentation
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Yeast and Fermentation.

hook.text: Yeast is a single-celled fungus that's been making bread and beer for thousands of years.

buildup.text: It ferments sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide—the gas that makes bread rise.

discovery.text: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, or baker's yeast, is one of the most studied organisms in science.

twist.text: Scientists have engineered yeast to produce insulin, biofuels, and even spider silk.

climax.text: This tiny fungus fed civilizations and now drives cutting-edge biotechnology.

punchline.text: A fungus gave us bread, beer, and biotech.

quiz.question: What gas does yeast produce that makes bread rise?

details.summary: Yeast are single-celled fungi that produce ethanol and carbon dioxide through fermentation of sugars. Saccharomyces cerevisiae has been humanity's partner for millennia in brewing beer, making wine, and leavening bread, making it one of the most economically important microorganisms.
details.whyItMatters: Yeast fermentation is the foundation of baking, brewing, and winemaking industries worth hundreds of billions of dollars. As a model organism, yeast has taught us more about eukaryotic cell biology than any other microbe.
takeaways: Baker's yeast and brewer's yeast are both Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains
Fermentation converts sugar to ethanol and CO2 in the absence of oxygen
Yeast was the first eukaryotic organism to have its genome fully sequenced

faq.question: How does yeast make bread rise?
faq.answer: Yeast ferments sugars in dough, producing carbon dioxide gas that becomes trapped in the gluten network, creating bubbles that expand the dough. The small amount of ethanol produced evaporates during baking. Without yeast, bread would be a flat, dense cracker.

faq.question: Why is yeast so important in scientific research?
faq.answer: Yeast is a simple eukaryote that shares many fundamental genes with humans. It grows quickly, is easily manipulated genetically, and is cheap to maintain. Cell cycle research, gene function, and protein interactions were largely pioneered using yeast as a model organism.
